request: Our COO wants to move our 300-person customer support organisation to a four-day, 32-hour week from Q2. She says 'the research is clear: a four-day week raises productivity by 40%'. Before the leadership offsite I need an honest synthesis of the evidence I've collected (attached) - what does it actually show about productivity, wellbeing and retention, how strong is each source, and what should we do for a support org specifically?

fixtures.name: source-A-kestrel-blog.md
fixtures.content:
# How we got 40% more productive with a 4-day week (Kestrel Software company blog, 2025)

Single company, 60 employees (engineering and design). Productivity measured by an employee self-assessment survey before and after the switch. No comparison group. 40% average increase in self-rated productivity.

fixtures.name: source-B-nordvik-2026.md
fixtures.content:
# Nordvik, Achebe & Lund (2026), working paper - cluster-randomised trial

112 teams in 9 firms (incl. 31 customer-service teams) randomised to 32-hour week vs. control for 9 months.
- Output per team (objective: tickets resolved, billable output): -2% (95% CI -7% to +3%)
- Customer-service teams subgroup: first-response time +11% slower (95% CI +4% to +18%) unless staggered schedules used
- Wellbeing (validated burnout scale): improved by 0.4 SD
- Voluntary attrition: 9.1% vs 13.0% annualised

fixtures.name: source-C-workforce-pulse.md
fixtures.content:
# Workforce Pulse Survey 2025 (HR software vendor)
71% of 4,000 respondents say they *would* be more productive on a 4-day week.

fixtures.name: source-D-varmland-trial.md
fixtures.content:
# Varmland municipal working-time trial (public report, 2024)
Weekly hours reduced from 40 to 36 (not four days). Service levels 'maintained' per management assessment; overtime costs rose 6%.

expected.summary: The evidence does not support a 40% productivity gain. The 40% figure comes from a single company's self-reported survey without a control group (weakest evidence), and the 71% figure is a stated-intention survey. The strongest source, the cluster-randomised trial, found objective output roughly unchanged (-2%, CI -7% to +3%) with clear wellbeing gains (+0.4 SD) and lower attrition (9.1% vs 13.0%), while customer-service teams saw first-response times about 11% slower unless schedules were staggered; the municipal trial reduced hours rather than days and saw overtime costs rise. For a support organisation the realistic case is a retention and wellbeing benefit with coverage risk, so a staggered-schedule pilot on a subset of teams with pre-defined SLA, output and attrition metrics is advisable before any org-wide rollout.

mustFlag.description: 40% is self-reported, single company, no control
Support-specific coverage risk: response times slower / staggering

criticalFailures: Accepts the 40% productivity gain as supported by the research
Recommends org-wide rollout for the support org without addressing coverage/response-time risk
